title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, likely sealing rate hike
description: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesInflation moved further away from the Federal Reser
body: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesInflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal.Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. However, it leaves unanswered how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, likely sealing rate hike

title: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state
description: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its t
body: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges."Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled."Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X. "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction. The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state

title: Crypto talent will return ‘when AI implodes,’ Arthur Hayes says
description: Arthur Hayes, the former chief executive officer of BitMEX, at the Consensus: Invest event in New York, U.S., on Tuesday, Nov. 28, 2017.Michael Nagle
body: Arthur Hayes, the former chief executive officer of BitMEX, at the Consensus: Invest event in New York, U.S., on Tuesday, Nov. 28, 2017.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesStartup talent that has concentrated in artificial intelligence will return to the crypto industry "when AI implodes," according to Arthur Hayes, chief investment officer at Maelstrom Fund."A lot of talent has gone into the AI space, so I definitely think there'll be a resurgence in good founder talent coming back to crypto," Hayes said in an online interview with CNBC on Tuesday.He added that some founders may also return once they "recognize" that their products could eventually be "usurped by Anthropic or OpenAI."The scale and capabilities of the largest frontier AI labs have made it difficult to "build a real AI business," Hayes said, arguing that "most" founders simply "raise a bunch of money and then light it on fire." He expects the AI trade to face "serious headwinds" in the second half of 2027, when leading labs begin confronting sizable bills tied to compute leases and other non-cancelable commitments. Anthropic expects about $451.6 billion in compute and infrastructure obligations through the end of 2030, with roughly $70.7 billion due by the end of September 2027, according to its prospectus."Do they have the money? We're going to find out," Hayes said.Broader enthusiasm around the AI trade has also cooled amid questions about future infrastructure spending. Even exuberance from Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO on Monday proved short-lived, with the shares falling 5.9% on Tuesday and Anthropic dropping below its IPO price four days after its debut. Bitcoin fall might continueThe co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX also thinks bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to fall. The cryptocurrency has shown little sign of recovery after dropping as low as $55,142.16 on Saturday — its lowest level since July.Bitcoin hit an all-time high of $126,279.63 in October last year and traded as high as $97,915.90 in January this year. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBitcoin prices were at an all-time high of $126,279.63 in October last year and were as high as $97,915.90 in January in the year to date.It has now fallen for seven straight weeks — only the third such streak in its history — with crypto exchange Bitfinex attributing the weakness to equity-market sentiment rather than interest-rate expectations.Hayes said he would like to see bitcoin rebound from around $55,000 even as the Nasdaq continues to fall. That divergence, he said, would suggest markets were shifting from a broad sell-off toward pricing in a "reflation" scenario, with the Federal Reserve eventually providing more liquidity.Neither bitcoin nor gold has yet decoupled from the Nasdaq, with Hayes describing the current market moves as a "correlation-led liquidation.""Stuff goes down, you sell crypto first because it's easy, and then you sell everything else," he said. Once that pattern changes, Hayes said he would be interested in owning Zcash, which he described as a "high beta bitcoin" with a greater focus on privacy, as well as ENA, the token of Ethereum-based platform Ethena.Hayes said a bitcoin rally could push up funding rates and futures-basis returns, increasing the income Ethena earns from its hedged crypto positions. That could make USDe, Ethena's synthetic dollar, more attractive and expand its circulation, he said, adding that he expects the ENA token to rise materially."Those are the two things that I'm keeping an eye on, and when I'm ready to pull the trigger on buying risk again, those will be the things we buy a lot of," Hayes said.

schema.headline: Crypto talent will return ‘when AI implodes,’ Arthur Hayes says

title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
description: Trucks move goods in a shipping container next to large stacks of shipping containers and cranes at the Port of Long Beach  Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026.
body: Trucks move goods in a shipping container next to large stacks of shipping containers and cranes at the Port of Long Beach  Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Allen J. Schaben | Los Angeles Times | Getty ImagesThe U.S. has proposed new tariffs on 14 partners including China, the European Union, Japan and India, as President Donald Trump doubles down on levies, despite a large chunk of his previous duties being struck down by the Supreme Court.The targeted economies create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors which burden or restrict American commerce, a senior U.S. official said.The 14 partners have been notified of these actions, with neither country's tariffs exceeding rates announced as part of framework deals on reciprocal trade, the official added.The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for China, which faces a 20% tariff on top of the 25% imposed in 2018 over forced technology transfers.The new duties on the world's second-largest economy could jump to 40% if it does not hold up its end of the trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in Oct. 2025, after which tariffs on Chinese exports to the U.S. were slashed to 47%.The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers."The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said on Wednesday before the official reports were released by the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.The new levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to counter foreign trade practices deemed unfair, discriminatory, or burdensome to U.S. commerce.CNBC earlier reported that the new tariffs would be "country specific," rather than a blanket rate, citing a source familiar with the matter. Tariffs have been a signature of the Trump administration since the president unveiled sweeping "Liberation Day" duties in April 2025 before pausing them after a sour reaction from bond markets. In February, the Supreme Court struck down tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.Trump used Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff after the court's decision, before replacing them with levies of up to 12.5% on 60 economies under Section 301, alleging forced labor practices.

schema.headline: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU

title: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast
description: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Ab
body: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Abu Dhabi on March 3, 2026. Iran stepped up its attacks on economic targets and US missions across the Middle East on March 3, as the US president warned it was "too late" for the Islamic republic to seek talks to escape the war. As drones and missiles crashed into oil facilities and US embassies in the Gulf, Washington's ally Israel bombarded targets in Iran and pushed troops deeper into Lebanon to battle the Tehran-backed militia Hezbollah. (Photo by Ryan Lim / AFP via Getty Images)Ryan Lim | Afp | Getty ImagesThe UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago. "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month shows that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy.He said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year. The Iran war has disrupted economic activity in the UAE, with missile and drone attacks from Tehran and maritime disruptions weighing on energy trade, tourism, aviation and private-sector confidence.Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump said that renewed attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a "very strong agreement." However, on Monday, Trump threatened that Tehran could face fresh U.S. strikes next year if the two countries failed to strike a deal, as per Fox News.   "We can we cannot promise the world for any storms that will land on our shore, but we can always promise that the UAE's economy is ready for any storm," Al Marri said. He added that next year the UAE's economy will have a "different" model than the one before the conflict and investments will be focused on building factories and "things that we really need in times of crisis."The World Bank in October said it expects the UAE's economy to recover next year, driven by rising oil production and exports and a rebound in tourism, trade, transportation, financial services, and construction. It warned that the improvement in economic activity in the UAE largely depends on the duration and intensity of the Iran war, with a faster de-escalation likely to accelerate the recovery in services exports and private-sector activity.

schema.headline: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast

title: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11
description: The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, center, in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday, Dec. 6, 2022. Bloo
body: The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, center, in the King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday, Dec. 6, 2022. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesYemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11. The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack. This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties. Red Sea threatsOn Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.  Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday, according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25, according to reports.The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet."As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X. The ministry later said two people, a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11

title: U.S. jury convicts Huawei in a criminal trial over fraud and trade secrets
description: Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChinese technology giant Huawei was convicted Tuesday in New York on multiple federal criminal charges, includi
body: Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChinese technology giant Huawei was convicted Tuesday in New York on multiple federal criminal charges, including fraud, U.S. sanctions violations and conspiracy to steal trade secrets, following a three-month trial, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.The verdict marks a major development in a long-running criminal case against Huawei, with charges first publicly disclosed in 2019.A federal jury found Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of multiple offenses, including bank and wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, the Justice Department said in a statement."No person or company is above the law," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said, accusing Huawei and its subsidiaries of conducting business in the United States through deception and theft.The Justice Department said Huawei misrepresented its activities in Iran to banks to secure billions of dollars and retain access to U.S. dollar-clearing services. The company also supplied surveillance cameras that enabled Iranian authorities to monitor protests, the department said.Among the examples of intellectual property theft detailed by prosecutors were cases involving Cisco and T-Mobile.Huawei copied source code used in Cisco routers, with its engineers referring to Cisco by spelling its name backward in an attempt to conceal the theft.Huawei employees also sent photographs and technical details of T-Mobile's touchscreen-testing robot to China, with one employee later removing a component from T-Mobile's laboratory in a backpack, according to the Justice Department."For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception," said Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division.Huawei pushed back against the verdict in a statement issued Wednesday, while welcoming its acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge."We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," Huawei said, adding that the five trade secret-related disputes cited by prosecutors had previously been resolved as civil matters.The company said it would review the verdicts and take necessary legal action to defend its interests, while remaining focused on maintaining uninterrupted business operations and investing in research and development.Huawei and its subsidiaries face potential financial penalties, including fines, forfeiture and restitution, with sentencing scheduled for Sept. 14, 2027, according to the Justice Department.U.S. prosecutors first publicly disclosed criminal charges against Huawei in January 2019, a month after the company's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, was arrested in Canada. Meng returned to China in September 2021 after entering into a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. prosecutors.

schema.headline: U.S. jury convicts Huawei in a criminal trial over fraud and trade secrets

title: Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeAbdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk."We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "includingdozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article. This is developing news. Check back for updates.

schema.headline: Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond

title: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist
description: A couple looks at a frozen food display while shopping at a Costco Wholesale store on Sept. 25, 2026 in Colchester, Vermont. Robert Nickelsberg | Gett
body: A couple looks at a frozen food display while shopping at a Costco Wholesale store on Sept. 25, 2026 in Colchester, Vermont. Robert Nickelsberg | Getty ImagesConsumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections, with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2.Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups.While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.The survey comes with the Federal Reserve continuing to try to bring down inflation, which has run above the central bank's 2% target for some 5½ years. The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point when it meets again in two weeks.Despite the lingering worries about the cost of living — a centerpiece issue during the midterms — the survey's present situation and expectations indexes both posted strong gains. Inflation expectations for 12 months from now fell for the second straight month but remained high at 5.7%.The survey's closely watched gap between jobs considered "plentiful" versus "hard to get" widened to 12.4 percentage points. The "plentiful" side rose to 30.8% from 26.2% while "hard to get" fell to 18.4%, down 3 percentage points.The survey results are the second in the past week to reveal that Americans are growing more optimistic about the economy. The University of Michigan's November survey, released Friday, showed a 7.3% increase since October, with a similar partisan split.

schema.headline: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist

title: China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel says
description: A conceptual image depicting the strained relationship between India and China, symbolized by their respective national flags painted on cracked and w
body: A conceptual image depicting the strained relationship between India and China, symbolized by their respective national flags painted on cracked and weathered surfaces, separated by a jagged, dividing line. Zpagistock | Moment | Getty ImagesChina is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India.China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense. Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.Chinese disruptionThe thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles, they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports. On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures. India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China, up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products. While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

schema.headline: China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel says

title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
description: Students Experience Virtual Reality At National Science Popularization Event In NanningChina News Service | China News Service | Getty ImagesBEIJING —
body: Students Experience Virtual Reality At National Science Popularization Event In NanningChina News Service | China News Service | Getty ImagesBEIJING — Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent."We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during a Bloomberg Television interview in London, UK, on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026.Jose Sarmento Matos | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMore than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said."Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.Big salary gapAlready, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations. In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S.," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options. "There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company. 'Huge' demandThe U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.  "The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex-Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

schema.headline: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips

title: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation
description: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow
body: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on November 6, 2026.Mikhail Metzel | Afp | Getty ImagesUkrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has told Russian President Vladimir Putin to "stop complaining" over attacks on Russian refineries, saying Putin could end Kyiv's strikes on the oil facilities by bringing an end to the Kremlin's nearly five-year-long war.His comments come shortly after Russia's president told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack refining facilities despite U.S. President Donald Trump's appeal to refrain from doing so. "I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency Tass. In September, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran propelled U.S. diesel prices to a record high. Moscow welcomed Trump's push for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russia's diesel-producing facilities at the time. "If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war," Ukraine's Sybiha said Tuesday via social media."If he doesn't want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war. Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," he added. CNBC could not independently verify the figures.In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that about 1.4 million Russian troops were killed, wounded or went missing between the start of the full-scale invasion in Feb. 2022 and June 2026, with more than 30,000 casualties a month in the first half of this year.Satellite view of thick black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara Oblast, Russia, on October 30, 2026.Gallo Images | Gallo Images | Getty ImagesUkraine has stepped up attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Putin's prized Crimea bridge, striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port.Kyiv has also targeted Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Ukraine's long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity, describing this as a "justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on our energy infrastructure."Putin: Fuel supply situation remains 'challenging'Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two major Russian oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, triggering fires at both facilities. Satellite images published in late October also showed black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in southern Russia following a suspected Ukrainian drone attack.   Putin on Tuesday said Russia's fuel market situation remains "challenging" and called on government officials and oil executives "to continue reacting promptly to the supply-demand relationship for fuel across the whole territory of Russia," according to Interfax.Ukraine's allies have warned the country faces another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures amid escalating Russian energy strikes.

schema.headline: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation

title: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value
description: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand
body: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.The shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials."I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY Parthenon, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality."It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added."It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said. Roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated."It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she said. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year."Emphasis on valueThe trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation."You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive."And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed said secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones. Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one."I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved."According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.Iannone said he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year."It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said. The era of personalizationFound Boston vintage market at the former SoWa Power Station, March 29, 2026.Matthew J. Lee | Boston Globe | Getty ImagesAt a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too."Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The company's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece. "To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem said — something unique.That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too. "Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds."Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen said. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date. "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen said. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue."

schema.headline: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

title: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
description: Dell Technologies demonstrates its technology at its exhibition booth during the 15th Smart Tech Korea exhibition at COEX in Seoul, South Korea, on Ju
body: Dell Technologies demonstrates its technology at its exhibition booth during the 15th Smart Tech Korea exhibition at COEX in Seoul, South Korea, on June 10, 2026, as visitors explore the company's displays and exhibits.Chris Jung | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesDell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter. Dell shares rose in extended trading. Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:EPS: $9.45, adjusted, versus $6.59 expectedRevenue: $54.94 billion, versus $49.32 billion expectedDell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD. ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue. "We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers. In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery."That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell. The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through. "Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts. The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion. The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as rising memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer. Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends. Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.Read more CNBC tech newsWhat Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette KressAnthropic stock falls below $83 IPO price, but analysts are still largely positiveNvidia brought Jensen Huang back. title: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
description: Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since
body: Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff, when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.Insmed shares closed up 14.1% at $170.15 on Tuesday, while Sanofi stock closed up 10.9% in Paris.'Buys time'Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete. Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026, as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026. While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconSanofi/Insmed shares over the past 12 months. "Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA, Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate, following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.Read more pharma newsA pharma giant is moving past one patent cliff — but another is already loomingEli Lilly hikes sales outlook, as CEO says there’s room for ‘dramatic’ obesity market expansionNovo’s new strategy hinges on something it can’t manufacture: investor trustCholesterol drug setback casts doubt over multibillion-dollar raceDoctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reactionAstraZeneca may buck a decade of pharma strategy to buy U.S. scaleTrump's generic drug tariffs: What they could mean for medicine prices, manufacturers and supplyNovo Nordisk sues Eli Lilly, alleging misleading GLP-1 advertisingNovo Nordisk's head start on GLP-1 pills forces investors to rethink Eli Lilly's dominancePrices, pipelines and patent cliffs: Inside pharma's big resetUK's biggest drugmakers see surprise profit bump, even as pharma grapples with U.S. policiesThe Insmed deal is a good strategic fit that will help soften the blow from Dupixent's expected 2031–32 loss of exclusivity, said Jefferies analysts. Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases."The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition. "Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement. Sanofi shares fell 2.9%, and Insmed rose 24% on Nov. 19 after Bloomberg reported that a deal was underway.

schema.headline: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
